nameStory: The Charcoal Eyelash gets its dramatic name from two key features: it appears on charcoal-black burn sites, and sports tiny brown hairs around its cup edges that look just like delicate eyelashes. The scientific name Anthracobia even means 'coal life,' perfectly capturing this little fungus's love affair with fire-scorched earth.
description: The Charcoal Eyelash is a small cup fungus that specializes in life after fire. It produces bright orangish, disc-like fruiting bodies that look like tiny shallow bowls or saucers scattered across burned ground. These distinctive cups are fringed with fine brown hairs around their rims, giving them their eyelash-like appearance. They're typically small enough to fit on a coin, making them easy to overlook despite their bright color.

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Always found on burn sites - old campfire rings, forest fire areas, or places where brush was burned; the orangish cups seem to glow against the blackened soil and charcoal

idTips.label: Cup Shape
idTips.description: Shallow, disc-like cups that feel firm but slightly flexible when gently pressed; they're saucer-shaped rather than deeply bowl-like

idTips.label: Orange Color
idTips.description: Bright orangish interior that catches the eye against dark burned substrates; the color is vibrant and warm, like a sunset

idTips.label: Brown Eyelashes
idTips.description: Tiny brown hairs fringe the cup edges, visible as a soft fuzzy border when viewed closely; they feel slightly bristly to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to sit comfortably on a quarter, rarely getting much larger than a nickel; they often appear in scattered groups rather than alone

habitat: Found exclusively in areas that have experienced burning - old campfire sites, forest burn areas, brush piles that were burned, or anywhere wood and organic matter has been charred. Prefers the actual burned soil and charcoal debris rather than nearby unburned areas. Most commonly spotted in wooded areas of New England where controlled burns or natural fires have occurred.

seasonality.spring: Prime fruiting season as soil warms; look for the bright orange cups emerging from last year's burn sites, especially after spring rains.
seasonality.summer: May continue producing fruit bodies in consistently moist burn sites, though they're less common during dry spells.
seasonality.fall: Occasionally fruits during wet autumn weather, but much less reliably than in spring.
seasonality.winter: No visible fruiting bodies; the fungus persists underground in burned soil, waiting for favorable conditions.

funFact: This little fungus is essentially a phoenix of the mushroom world - it won't even consider growing unless the ground has been burned, making it completely dependent on fire for its lifecycle and earning it the nickname 'bonfire cup' among some mushroom hunters.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small orange cup fungi, but the burn site habitat is a dead giveaway - if it's not growing on burned ground, it's not a Charcoal Eyelash. Remember: 'No char, not far' - this species simply won't appear anywhere else.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'cup fungus' refers to the shape of the fruiting body, not actual cups you'd drink from. These fungi are part of a large group called 'apothecial fungi,' where 'apothecium' simply means the cup or disc-shaped structure that holds the spores.
compareHints: Since Charcoal Eyelash is the only Anthracobia species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small orange cup fungi in the Pyronemataceae family. Unlike most of its relatives, Charcoal Eyelash is completely restricted to burn sites and has the distinctive brown eyelash hairs. Other orange cups in the family typically grow on soil, dung, or decaying matter but avoid burned areas entirely.
